title: The Language of the reservoir
premise: Coral Okafor, a piano tuner who inherited her grandmother's house and her silence in equal measure, drifts through rooms she has never claimed as her own. When Adaora Eze, the last fluent speaker of Ọ̀nà, a dying Nigerian language, asks Coral to become her final student, the lessons become an excavation of everything Coral has refused to say — about her grandmother, about Tomás, the man she left rather than marry, about the word for grief she never learned. As Adaora's health fails, Coral must record the language before it vanishes, but recording means speaking, and speaking means finally saying goodbye to her grandmother out loud. The novel ends with Adaora's death and Coral's choice: she teaches Ọ̀nà to a classroom of strangers, becoming not the last speaker but the first of a new line.
about_author: Jude Thornbury is the pen name of a former radio archivist who spent a decade cataloguing endangered-language recordings in West Africa. They now write from a house with very loud radiators.

chapters.title: The Tenant
chapters.summary: Coral Okafor tunes pianos across the city, reading houses through their radiators and pipes, but treats her late grandmother's house like rented space — unopened boxes, untouched piano. POV: Coral. Emotional beat: quiet displacement; she owns nothing she inhabits, including her own history.

chapters.title: A Word for Grief
chapters.summary: At a community center recital, Coral meets Adaora Eze, who identifies Coral's grandmother's dialect from a hummed lullaby Coral doesn't know she knows. Adaora reveals she is the last speaker of Ọ̀nà and asks for one student. POV: Coral. Beat: startled recognition — something in her answers before she can refuse.

chapters.title: First Lesson
chapters.summary: Coral visits Adaora's apartment, dense with cassette tapes and labeled jars. The first lesson is only listening: Adaora speaks and refuses translation. Coral realizes the language sounds like her grandmother's kitchen. POV: Coral. Beat: reluctant hunger; she wants what she swore not to want.

chapters.title: What the Radiators Said
chapters.summary: Coral tunes a piano in the house where she grew up and overhears, through its pipes, a family argument that isn't hers — a mirror of her own unfinished one. She begins opening her grandmother's boxes at night. POV: Coral. Beat: the past knocking; first crack in her tenancy of avoidance.

chapters.title: Tomás
chapters.summary: Tomás Reyes reappears — the man Coral left eleven years ago when duty to her dying grandmother outweighed love. He repairs the center's heating and their radiators literally speak over each other. POV: Coral. Beat: old love resurfacing as accusation and tenderness at once.

chapters.title: Tones
chapters.summary: Adaora teaches tones: meaning changes with pitch, the same syllable as blessing or curse. Coral, a tuner, grasps it instantly — and hears how long she has been saying her own words in the wrong key. POV: Coral. Beat: craft becomes metaphor; skill turns inward.

chapters.title: The Boxes
chapters.summary: Coral finds her grandmother's letters, unsent, written in Ọ̀nà script — decades of correspondence to a sister in Nigeria who never replied. Her grandmother had a whole voice Coral never heard. POV: Coral. Beat: betrayal and wonder braided together; inheritance revealed as buried speech.

chapters.title: Adaora's Terms
chapters.summary: Adaora collapses briefly and hides it. She sets terms: if Coral learns, she must promise to pass the language on — no private museum pieces. Coral hesitates; she can't even claim her own house. POV: alternating Coral/Adaora. Beat: contract and foreshadowing; duty enters the room.

chapters.title: Recording
chapters.summary: Coral brings her old radio equipment and begins taping Adaora — vocabulary, songs, jokes. Hearing her own voice on tape saying new words, Coral weeps without deciding to. POV: Coral. Beat: preservation begins; grief given a container.

chapters.title: The Sister's Grandson
chapters.summary: Coral writes to the address on the letters and reaches Chidi, her grandmother's great-nephew in Enugu, who replies in careful English: the family believed the grandmother had abandoned them. POV: Coral. Beat: the price of survival named — her grandmother chose silence to survive emigration.

chapters.title: Duty's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Adaora's POV: 1960s Lagos, her choice between joining her husband's political exile and staying with her language community; she stayed, and watched everyone else leave or die. Beat: Adaora's parallel wound — she also paid survival's price, in a different currency.

chapters.title: Interlude: The House Speaks
chapters.summary: A short lyric chapter from the house's perspective — pipes, floorboards, the sealed piano — registering Coral's presence changing: boxes opened, windows washed, the piano lid lifted. Beat: stillness and turning; the tenant becoming resident.

chapters.title: Tomás Again
chapters.summary: Tomás and Coral repair the community center's ancient boiler together. He asks why she left; she says 'duty' and hears, in Adaora's tonal lesson, how flat the word comes out. POV: Coral. Beat: rising tension — love demanding a real answer this time.

chapters.title: Chidi Arrives
chapters.summary: Chidi visits, carrying his grandmother's reply to letters sent fifty years ago — found unopened after her death. Two silences, two continents, one family. He and Coral sit with Adaora, who translates the letters aloud. POV: Coral. Beat: catharsis deferred then delivered; the dead begin speaking.

chapters.title: The Word She Never Learned
chapters.summary: Adaora teaches the Ọ̀nà word for goodbye-that-means-until-again. Coral cannot pronounce it; her throat closes. Adaora diagnoses it plainly: you are keeping your grief as evidence. POV: Coral. Beat: crisis of the interior plot — the language demands surrender.

chapters.title: Hospital
chapters.summary: Adaora is hospitalized. Recording sessions move to her bedside; nurses learn greetings; the ward fills with a language only two people fully share, one of them fading. POV: alternating. Beat: urgency compresses everything; time audibly running out.

chapters.title: The Argument
chapters.summary: Coral and Tomás fight — he accuses her of choosing archives over people again, as she once chose duty over him. She storms out, then sits all night with the tapes and understands he is right. POV: Coral. Beat: climax of the relational thread; the pattern made undeniable.

chapters.title: Saying It Out Loud
chapters.summary: Coral returns to the hospital and, in Ọ̀nà, says goodbye to her grandmother aloud at last — the full unsent letter read back into the room, Adaora translating each line. Then she tells Tomás the truth: she was afraid, not dutiful. POV: Coral. Beat: emotional climax; speech as resurrection.

chapters.title: Last Lesson
chapters.summary: Adaora, home on hospice care, gives her final lesson: not vocabulary but how to teach — patience, repetition, joy. She makes Coral promise again, and this time Coral promises in Ọ̀nà. POV: Adaora. Beat: transmission completed; the torch passed while both hands can hold it.

chapters.title: Adaora
chapters.summary: Adaora dies on a Sunday morning with the tapes playing. Coral sits with the body and speaks to her in Ọ̀nà — imperfect, unafraid. The community center fills for the funeral; strangers ask what the language was. POV: Coral. Beat: elegy; grief finally fluent.

chapters.title: The First Class
chapters.summary: Six weeks later, Coral opens the sealed piano in her grandmother's house — now unmistakably hers — and teaches Ọ̀nà to nine students including Tomás and Chidi's daughter via video call. Her pronunciation falters; nobody minds. POV: Coral. Beat: resolution; inheritance accepted and multiplied.

chapters.title: Until Again
chapters.summary: Epilogue: a year on, Coral records her students' voices beside Adaora's tapes, labels them in two scripts, and mails copies to Enugu. The radiators sing; the house is full. She ends a letter with the goodbye-that-means-until-again. POV: Coral. Beat: quiet continuance; loss converted into lineage.
